title: Harun al-Rashid and the Noble Widow of the Barmecides
summary: Following the tragic fall of the illustrious Barmecide family in Baghdad, when their palaces were sealed and their estates confiscated, the Caliph Harun al-Rashid prohibited any...

full_text:
Following the tragic fall of the illustrious Barmecide family in Baghdad, when their palaces were sealed and their estates confiscated, the Caliph Harun al-Rashid prohibited any citizen from reciting elegies in praise of their former generosity.

One morning, as the Caliph was walking through the garden quarter, an elderly lady wrapped in a frayed, clean woollen mantle stepped before him. Though dressed in poverty, her bearing was that of a queen, and her eyes shone with unyielding dignity.

She recited aloud in a ringing, melodious voice:
'May heaven grant you, O Caliph, the exact measure of justice that you have meted out to the house of Barmak!'

Harun al-Rashid frowned, his hand resting upon his scimitar: 'Do you pray for me, woman, or do you curse me?'

The lady replied with fearless composure: 'I prayed that justice may be your reward, O Commander of the Faithful. If you dealt with them in truth and equity, my prayer is a blessing; but if you broke the vessels of generosity, exiled your truest friends, and left their widows to beg for bread, then my prayer is the judgment of history upon your throne.'

The words struck the Caliph like an iron mace! He recognized her: she was the noble widow of Yahya bin Khalid.

Tears of profound remorse welled in Harun al-Rashid’s eyes. He bowed before her, ordered an annual pension of ten thousand dinars to be settled upon her household, and restored her ancestral home, having learned that true nobility speaks truth to power without fear of death.
moral: Poetic eloquence and moral dignity disarm the wrath of monarchs, commanding respect and justice.
